name: Piratapuyo
confidence_why: Two independent field teams, Klumpp & Klumpp 1973 and Waltz & Waltz 1987/2015, both describe Piratapuyo as a two-tone (high/low) language whose stress coincides with high tone, and Cezario 2025 reports Picanço 2019 analysing Wa'ikhana as a tone language with root melodies; the only difference is whether stress is stated as falling on the first high-tone syllable (Klumpp & Klumpp) or on the last syllable of the root, which carries the high tone (Waltz & Waltz).

catalog_quote: 5.1 Tono. Los dos tonos fonémicos son alto, marcado /´/ y bajo, que no se marca. duhíyá 'siéntese!', duhíya 'aterrice!' ... wąbę́ 'tía', wą́bę́ 'nombre', okóró 'lluvia', okóro 'paraguas' ... El tono alto y el acento ocurren simultáneamente. En palabras con más de una sílaba con tono alto, cada tono alto subsiguiente es un poco más alto que el precedente. Sobre la primera sílaba con tono alto ocurren un acento un poco más fuerte y un alargamiento opcional del núcleo. ipírí [ìI'pí'ří] 'dientes', basáhá [bàA'sá'há] 'canto', peórí [pē'ó'ĺí] 'rápidos', tíkóró ['tí'kó'řó] 'ella' ... [p.114] 7. Grupos acentuales (palabras fonológicas). Aunque los límites de las palabras en piratapuyo no son totalmente predecibles en términos fonológicos, el acento y el tono son dos rasgos que ayudan a segmentar un flujo de habla en palabras, definidas aquí como grupos acentuales. En general, la palabra tiene una sílaba con un acento principal. Los modelos tonales también ayudan a describir la palabra fonológica. La gran mayoría de las palabras caen en uno de los siguientes modelos tonales: ´, `´, `´`, `´´, `´, `´´´. Los siguientes modelos son raros: ´´, ´`, ´´`, ´, ´´´, ´`. [p.117] ... La mayoría de las palabras tienen de una a cuatro sílabas, aunque hay unos pocos ejemplos de cinco, seis y hasta de siete sílabas. [p.118]

new_statements.translation: 5.1 Tone. The two phonemic tones are high, marked /´/, and low, which is unmarked. [...] High tone and stress occur simultaneously. In words with more than one high-toned syllable, each subsequent high tone is a little higher than the preceding one. On the first high-toned syllable there occur a somewhat stronger stress and an optional lengthening of the nucleus. [p.114] ... In general, the word has one syllable with a primary stress. The tonal patterns also help to describe the phonological word. The great majority of words fall into one of the following tonal patterns: H, LH, LHL, LHH, LHLL, LHHH. The following patterns are rare: HH, HL, HHL, HLL, HHH, HLLL. [p.117]

new_statements.rule_in_words: Two-tone (H/L) system; stress is not independent of tone: the primary word stress falls on the first high-toned syllable of the phonological word (with optional lengthening), later H syllables being slightly higher in pitch but less stressed. Since the common word melodies are L H(…) and bare H, primary stress is most often on the second syllable, sometimes the first. Waltz & Waltz 2015 (p.2) state the same distribution morphologically: regular word stress falls on the last syllable of the root (roots mostly disyllabic), tone being marked separately only for tonal minimal pairs.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Klumpp & Klumpp: subsequent high-toned syllables are each slightly higher in pitch but the first H carries the stronger stress. Waltz 2012 dictionary (p.5): if a word or phrase contains more than one stress, the following ones are secondary.
new_statements.exceptions: Waltz & Waltz 2015 p.2: the negative suffix -era [ˈera] and the negative-imperative suffix -é always carry the word stress (exceptions to root-final stress); Waltz 2012 §3.1.4 repeats '-era- lleva el acento de la palabra'. Klumpp & Klumpp list rare initial-H patterns (HH, HL, HHL, HLL, HHH, HLLL). Cezario 2025 (after Picanço 2019): root melodies H, HL, LH, LHL with rightward spreading onto toneless suffixes.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the 'grupo acentual' = phonological word (root plus suffixes, 1-4 syllables typically, up to 7), delimited by stress, tone pattern, the breathy pre-H syllable and potential pause (K&K §7). Examples are citation forms and short utterances. Phrase-level emphatic stress/lengthening is described separately (§8, frase D).
new_statements.identity_note: Both SIL sources (Klumpp & Klumpp 1973; Waltz & Waltz 2015; Waltz 2012) describe 'piratapuyo' as spoken on the Papurí river, Vaupés, Colombia; the Brazilian works (Picanço 2019, Cezario 2025, Balykova 2019) use the autonym Wa'ikhana for the same language (pira1254, ISO pir). No dialect split is claimed in the sources read.

new_statements.quote: Piratapuyo tiene dos tonos: el tono alto que se marca con un acento en la fonética y en pares minimales en la ortografía; y el tono bajo que no se marca. Por lo general, un tono alto ocurre en la sílaba acentuada. La posición del acento es predicible gramáticalmente y por lo general cae en la última sílaba de la raíz en verbos, sustantivos y adjetivos [...] Excepciones incluyen ciertos sufijos que siempre llevan el acento de una palabra, entre ellos /-éra/ ‘negativo’ [...] Otras excepciones son palabras con acentos múltiples que están pronunciado más o menos en un monótono [...] Además acentos multiples pueden ocurrir en una palabra phonológica cuando varios sufijos se añadan
new_statements.translation: Piratapuyo has two tones: the high tone, which is marked with an accent in the phonetic transcription and in minimal pairs in the orthography, and the low tone, which is not marked. In general, a high tone occurs on the stressed syllable. The position of the stress is grammatically predictable and generally falls on the last syllable of the root in verbs, nouns and adjectives [...] Exceptions include certain suffixes that always carry the stress of a word, among them /-éra/ 'negative' [...] Other exceptions are words with multiple stresses that are pronounced more or less in a monotone [...] Moreover, multiple stresses can occur in a phonological word when several suffixes are added [to the verb nucleus].

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Piratapuyo has an empty rule; the existing statement (Klumpp & Klumpp 1973) records a two-tone language in which high tone and stress occur together, with stress on the first high-tone syllable. Waltz & Waltz agree that Piratapuyo has two tones and that H tone and stress coincide, and add the placement rule the catalog lacks: stress is grammatically predictable and falls on the last syllable of the root, with the NEG suffix -éra as a stress-attracting exception and multiple stresses per phonological word. This matches the rule already noted held by the project from the same authors' 2015 Gramatica pedagogica p.2 ('El acento regular de la palabra cae en la ultima silab…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Two-tone language (H marked, L unmarked). High tone and stress coincide: the high tone generally sits on the stressed syllable. Stress placement is grammatically predictable and by default falls on the last syllable of the root (verbs, nouns, adjectives), i.e. a morphological root-final rule; examples /wekɨ/ 'loro', /sõʔã/ 'rojo' with stress/H on the final root syllable. Sec. 3.3 (p.9) adds that a vowel is deleted before a stressed vowel-initial morpheme (/iʔy(a)-e-re/ [iʔ yére]).
new_statements.secondary_stress: No 'secondary stress' as such; instead the work says a phonological word (up to eight syllables, sec. 2.2.2 p.5) is not limited to one stress and may carry multiple stresses ('acento múltiple'), both in some lexical items pronounced near-monotone (/akoro/ [aAkóró] 'lluvia', /keʔdõãrĩ/ 'bueno', /wãbẽ/ 'nombre') and when several suffixes are added to a verb (yaʔu-é-pe-gɨ-tá 'aunque él no lo explica').
new_statements.exceptions: (1) Certain suffixes always take the word stress, notably the negative /-éra/ (sec. 2.3.2 p.7; sec. 4.3.1.4 p.17: 'El sufijo [-éra-] lleva el acento de la palabra'). (2) Words with multiple stresses pronounced roughly in a monotone. (3) Multiple stresses in polymorphemic verb words.
new_statements.identity_note: The work describes Piratapuyo (Eastern Tucanoan, Vaupés region; speakers on the río Papurí, lower Vaupés and río Negro, Colombia and Brazil), the same language as the catalog item; no particular dialect is singled out. Data were collected by Nathan and Carolyn Waltz between 1987 and 2002 under SIL; the downloaded PDF is the 2015 first edition, which is why Glottolog dates it 2015 while the catalog citation says 1987.

tone_statements.citation: Picanço, Heitor Rui de Araújo. 2019. Aspectos fonológicos da língua Wa'ikhana (Tukano Oriental). Dissertação de mestrado, 150 pp. (Glottolog: Universidade do Estado do Amazonas; author later a UFRJ doctoral student per Cezario 2025).
tone_statements.quote: Ainda que não destrinchando toda sua complexidade tonal sujacente, tratamos a língua wa'ikhana como uma língua tonal, ancorando-nos na definição de Hyman (2001, p. 1368) [...] o tom em wa'ikhana se associa a morfemas, obrigatório, detém função distintiva e é paradigmático, com alinhamento à mora (ao contrário da sílaba) [...] Em wa'ikhana, as quatro melodias básicas contabilizadas são: A, AB, BA e BAB. Elas se associam da esquerda para direita em cada mora, unidade portadora do tom (ing. tone-bearing unit, TBU). Raízes são marcadas com, pelo menos, um tom A. Não há raízes somente especificadas com B.
tone_statements.translation: Although not unravelling all of its underlying tonal complexity, we treat Wa'ikhana as a tone language, relying on Hyman's (2001: 1368) definition [...] tone in Wa'ikhana associates to morphemes, is obligatory, has a distinctive function and is paradigmatic, aligned to the mora (rather than the syllable) [...] In Wa'ikhana the four basic melodies counted are H, HL, LH and LHL. They associate from left to right to each mora, the tone-bearing unit (TBU). Roots are marked with at least one H tone. There are no roots specified only with L.

readall_conflicts: No contradiction. Klumpp & Klumpp 1973 (existing statement) describe stress as a correlate of tone: high tone and stress occur simultaneously and the first high-tone syllable carries a somewhat stronger stress and optional lengthening. Waltz & Waltz (this work, and their 2015 pedagogical grammar already held by the project) describe the same coincidence from the other direction: the high tone generally occurs on the stressed syllable, and stress is grammatically predictable, falling on the last syllable of the root, with stress-attracting suffixes (NEG -éra) and multiple stresses in polymorphemic words. Both sources agree the language has two tones (H/L) and that stress and H tone co-occur; Waltz & Waltz's 'acentos múltiples' correspond to Klumpp & Klumpp's multi-H patterns (LHH, LHHH, etc.). The only difference is which of tone or morphological position is treated as primary, which is a matter of description, not of fact.

sources.note: Sec. 5.1 'Tono' (printed p.114): two phonemic tones, high (marked) and low; high tone and stress occur simultaneously; the first high-toned syllable carries a somewhat stronger stress and optional lengthening; later H syllables are each slightly higher in pitch. Sec. 7 'Grupos acentuales' (p.117-118): the phonological word generally has one main-stress syllable; common word tone patterns H, LH, LHL, LHH, LHLL, LHHH; rare HH, HL, HHL, HLL, HHH, HLLL (i.e. first H, hence main stress, is usually on the 2nd syllable).

Por ejemplo, waha [waꞌɁa] ir; maca [maAꞌká] pueblo. Unos excepciones son el sufijo negativo [ꞌera] y el sufiijo del mandato negativo [é] que siempre llevan el acento.. sources.citation: Cezario Soares, Bruna. 2025. Verbos seriais em Wa'ikhana (Tukano Oriental): uma abordagem construcionista. Tese de doutorado, Universidade Federal do Rio de Janeiro. 142 pp.
sources.note: pp.65-67 report Picanço (2019: 122-123) second-hand: Wa'ikhana is a tone language, tone aligns with the mora and is lexically distinctive; verbal roots are bimoraic with one of four melodies H, HL, LH, LHL; the root-final tone spreads over toneless suffixes; in serial-verb words the first root's melody governs the whole phonological word (Praat figures). Nothing on stress as distinct from tone.

tone.quote: Ainda que não destrinchando toda sua complexidade tonal sujacente, tratamos a língua wa'ikhana como uma língua tonal, ancorando-nos na definição de Hyman (2001, p. 1368) [...] o tom em wa'ikhana se associa a morfemas, obrigatório, detém função distintiva e é paradigmático, com alinhamento à mora (ao contrário da sílaba) [...] Em wa'ikhana, as quatro melodias básicas contabilizadas são: A, AB, BA e BAB. Elas se associam da esquerda para direita em cada mora, unidade portadora do tom (ing. tone-bearing unit, TBU). Raízes são marcadas com, pelo menos, um tom A. Não há raízes somente especificadas com B.
tone.locator: sec. 5.11.2 'Tom', pp.122-123; melodies sentence opens p.123
tone.translation: Although not unravelling all of its underlying tonal complexity, we treat Wa'ikhana as a tone language, relying on Hyman's (2001: 1368) definition [...] tone in Wa'ikhana associates to morphemes, is obligatory, has a distinctive function and is paradigmatic, aligned to the mora (rather than the syllable) [...] In Wa'ikhana the four basic melodies counted are H, HL, LH and LHL. They associate from left to right to each mora, the tone-bearing unit (TBU). Roots are marked with at least one H tone. There are no roots specified only with L.

tone.says: First-hand autosegmental analysis (sec. 5.3.3 'Oposições tonais' p.72-73; sec. 5.11.2 'Tom' pp.120-128): Wa'ikhana is treated as a tone language (Hyman's definition); two level tones A (high) and B (low); TBU = mora; four basic root melodies H, HL, LH, LHL associated left-to-right, every root has at least one H, no all-L roots, no LL sequences within a root; root-initial L in LH/LHL is extrametrical <L>; LH vs LHL (and H vs HL) on bimoraic roots are only distinguishable once a toneless suffix i…

tone.quote: As with nasalization, tone spreads in Kotiria and Wa’ikhana. The basic tonal patterns in Kotiria are tri-tonal. [...] There are four possible combinations for tone in Kotiria; LHL, LH, HL, and H. [...] There have not been any works published about tone in Wa’ikhana, however, it behaves in the same was as tone in Kotiria and all guidelines discussed for KOT may be applied to WAI (Stenzel, personal communication, 2015).

tone.says: Sec. 4.7.2 'Tone' (pp.28-30): only H and L tones in East Tukanoan; apparent contours are conditioned H; tone treated as a morpheme-level suprasegmental that spreads to toneless ('chameleon') suffixes like nasalization, spreading cannot be blocked; four melodies LHL, LH, HL, H starting at the left edge, third tone of a bimoraic root surfaces only under suffixation; states that nothing had been published on Wa'ikhana tone but that it behaves exactly like Kotiria tone (Stenzel p.c. 2015); Table 4.…
